segments.english: "The fifth: the people who dwell in Asia, if a written command from the king comes to them, they take it in their hands, kiss it with their mouths and place it on their heads. How much more so shall we honor the words of the living God, King over all the earth.
segments.literal: fifth the-people the-dwelling in-Asia if comes to-them written-command from-the-king in-their-hands they-seize-it, with-their-mouths they-kiss-it, and-on their-heads they-place-it, how-much-more so we-shall-honor the-words-of God living King over all the-earth

tokens.note: ordinal of a numbered series: 2:24 is the sixth, 2:25 the seventh
yiqtol after אם: the protasis of a conditional; the verbs that follow are yiqtol in a habitual sense
מכתב, 'letter, writing'
פקודה, an order
יתפשוהו: root תפש with the suffix ־הו, 'it'; the command is the object
אף כי: 'how much more so', the apodosis of an argument from the lesser to the greater
נכבד: cohortative, 'let us honor'
object marker את, no English
אלהים: the God of Israel, here 'the living God' (חיים)

phrases.english: The fifth: the people who dwell in Asia,
if a written command from the king comes to them,
they take it in their hands,
kiss it with their mouths,
and place it on their heads.
How much more so
shall we honor
the words of the living God,
King over all the earth.

grammar: The paragraph is the fifth point of a numbered series, and its number opens the English as it opens the Hebrew.
The conditional אם takes yiqtol verbs (they take, kiss, place): these describe a habitual practice, so the English uses the present.
The argument is from the lesser to the greater (qal wa-chomer): if the people honor a king's written command, 'how much more so' the words of God. The cohortative נכבד keeps the 'we shall'.
The three acts (seizing in the hands, kissing with the mouth, placing on the head) are parallel clauses, and the English keeps their order.
apparatus: Base text from Wikisource; the 1931 scan is not yet collated, so the paragraph is translated as the base text (decisions, Q2).
Quotation: the double quotation marks open at this segment because the quoted letter is closed by עכ"ל at 2:25. The opening formula is not in this unit.
Allusions, the author's wording and not a quotation: 'the living God' (Jer 10:10) and 'King over all the earth' (cf. Zech 14:9).

segments.english: The sixth: when the seventy-two elders brought the Torah to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, he rose from his throne and bowed down seven times to meet it, and if a worshipper of idols who has not put his neck under the yoke of our Torah, which is so heavy, how much more so we who enter into its covenant and to whom it was given as an inheritance.
segments.literal: sixth when-they-brought seventy and-two elders (object) the-Torah to-Ptolemy king of-Egypt rose from-his-throne and-bowed-down seven times to-meet-it, and-if worshipper-of idols who not put his-neck into-the-yoke of-our-Torah is-heavy so much, how-much-more so we entering in-its-covenant and-to-whom it-was-given to-us as-inheritance

tokens.note: כשהביאו: 'when' with a qatal; the verb comes before its subject
שבעים ושנים: seventy-two, written 'seventy and two'
object marker את, no English
תלמי, the Hebrew spelling of the king's name
מכסאו: 'from his throne'
והשתחוה: the act of reverence; the verb is the same as in 2:26
ז׳ is the numeral seven, not a letter
לקראתה: lit. 'to meet it', the greeting of a sacred object
עובד אלילים: 'worshipper of idols'
הביא צוארו בעול: lit. 'brought his neck into the yoke', an idiom of accepting a burden
בעול: the yoke, the image of taking on the Torah
כבדה: feminine, agreeing with תורתינו; the Torah is what is heavy, not the yoke
אף כי: 'how much more so', as in 2:23
הבאים: participle, 'who enter'
בבריתה: the covenant of the Torah; 'its' is the Torah
למורשה: 'as an inheritance'; see apparatus

phrases.english: The sixth:
when the seventy-two elders brought
the Torah
to Ptolemy, king of Egypt,
he rose from his throne
and bowed down seven times to meet it,
and if a worshipper of idols
who has not put his neck under the yoke of our Torah,
phrases.literal: who not brought his-neck into-the-yoke of-our-Torah

phrases.english: which is so heavy,
how much more so
we who enter into its covenant
and to whom it was given as an inheritance.

grammar: The temporal clause כשהביאו puts the verb first and the subject after it: 'when the seventy-two elders brought the Torah'.
קם ... והשתחוה are two past acts in sequence (qatal with vav); the English keeps the sequence, 'rose ... and bowed down'.
The clause introduced by ואם has no verb. The Hebrew leaves the king's act to be understood, and the English keeps the ellipsis; the apodosis 'how much more so we' answers it.
כבדה is feminine and agrees with תורתינו, so 'which is so heavy' describes the Torah, not the yoke.
apparatus: Allusion, not quoted: Deut 33:4 for 'למורשה' ('an inheritance').
The number seventy-two and the translation story are the author's (see context).
context: The Greek translation of the Torah, made in Alexandria in the third century BCE, is attributed in the rabbinic tradition to seventy-two elders in the time of Ptolemy, king of Egypt. The author follows that tradition.

segments.english: "Seventh: the foundation and principle of our religion is the existence of one, unique, eternal Creator, who is not a body, nor a force in a body, who gives the Torah to His people Israel through the faithful lawgiver Moses, servant of the LORD, master of all the prophets. He, may He be blessed, looks on and exercises providence over the worlds that He created. And His eyes roam over all, He searches and examines the hearts of the sons of man and judges justly according to the deeds, the steps of a man. From Him alone we seek help in our distress, and He will bring forth a shoot from the stock of Jesse, who will gather the outcasts of Israel from the four corners of the earth, and from all the cut-off corners to which they scattered them there, the dry bones of their dead will live, and their corpses will rise. Indeed, all these are the principles and roots of our religion. And what trace of idolatry is found in them? Even concerning those whose opinions and beliefs differ from our opinions and from our faith." Thus far his words.

grammar: The paragraph is one sentence: 'the foundation ... is the existence of ...'. Its relative clauses (אשר, נותן) continue from the Creator, and the English keeps the sentence long.
The verbs of providence (המציץ, ומשגיח, חוקר, ובוחן, ושופט) are participles with no finite verb; the English makes them finite with 'He'.
והוא יפרה נצר: Isa 11:1 has this verb intransitively ('shall bear fruit'); here it takes נצר as its object, and the English follows the author ('bring forth a shoot').
The last sentence has no verb ('even concerning those ...'); the English keeps the fragment, as the Hebrew does.
apparatus: Quotation: the double quotation marks close here with the formula עכ"ל. The opening is outside this unit (see 2:23 apparatus).

Allusions, the author's wording and not quotations: Jer 17:10 (חוקר לב בוחן) for 'searches and examines the hearts'; Prov 20:24 (מצעדי גבר) for 'the steps of a man'; Isa 11:1 for 'a shoot from the stock of Jesse'; Isa 11:12 (מארבע כנפות הארץ) for 'from the four corners of the earth'; Ezek 37 (the dry bones) and Isa 26:19 (נבלתי יקומון) for the resurrection clause; Jer 9:25 for 'cut-off corners'.
context: קצוצי פאה (Jer 9:25): the phrase names, in that verse, the peoples of the desert who cut the corners of their hair, a practice Lev 19:27 forbids to Israel. Here the phrase names the places to which Israel was scattered.

segments.english: And according to our way, the way of our Rabbis of blessed memory in the aforementioned baraita, there is no need for all this, since our intention is not that we bow down before the Torah scroll, but to Him who chose the Torah. Explicitly, we say: "Come, let us bow down and kneel, let us bless before the LORD our Maker." As for the bowing down of Abraham our father to the angels, and so Joshua's. If you wish, say: since they appeared to them as men, we apply to them what the Rabbis said in the baraita: "'You shall not bow down to them.' To them you may not bow down, but you bow down to a man like yourself," since they were revealed to them in the form of men. And if you wish, say: the intention of Abraham and Joshua was to bow down to Him who sent them, as the author of the Ikkarim wrote.

grammar: בואו נשתחוה ונכרעה נברכה is Ps 95:6, given as the people's words: the cohortatives ('let us') stay in the English, and the verse is set in quotation marks.
והשתחוית is a noun ('the bowing down'), so 'As for the bowing down' is a topic phrase; the English needs no verb until 'and so Joshua's'.

איבעית אימא ('if you wish, say') introduces a second explanation. The author gives two, the first (the angels appeared as men) and the second (the intention was toward the One who sent them); the English keeps both in order.
The baraita is quoted inside the sentence ('what the Rabbis said in the baraita: ...'), and the English returns to the author's syntax with 'since they were revealed to them'.
אי אתה משתחוה is the Talmudic negative of permission, 'you may not bow down'; the English keeps the modal.
apparatus: Ps 95:6 for 'בואו נשתחוה ונכרעה נברכה לפני ה׳ עושנו'.
Exod 20:5 for 'לא תשתחוה להם' ('you shall not bow down to them'), the words of the baraita.
Cf. Gen 18:2 and Josh 5:14 for the bowing of Abraham and Joshua; the author alludes to them and does not quote them.

segments.english: And your question concerning prophecy, although it does not belong to our subject, and you did not ask only to mislead us and to divert us to another matter. Behold, this is set out in the degrees of prophecy in the Rambam, Laws of the Foundations of the Torah, and in part two of the book Moreh Nevukhim, and in the book Emunot ve-De'ot of Rabbi Saadia Gaon. Since I have found you wise in your eyes, I return to ask you to answer me a decisive answer from the words of our Rabbis of blessed memory in the Talmud, for you alone (in your opinion) all mysteries have been revealed to you, and greater understanding, and a new spirit has been given within you. Instruct us, I and my companions, how the matters can agree fully and well. For our soul has longed to hear your teachings, and to delight in your perfect Torah, and it will be to you a merit, and also great honor you will inherit from us.

grammar: The paragraph is a single letter sentence, and the list of works (the Rambam, the Moreh, Emunot ve-De'ot) is a series of 'in' phrases; the English keeps the series in the Hebrew's order.
ולא שאלת רק להטעותנו: 'you did not ask except to mislead us'; the English keeps the restriction with 'only'.
חכם בעיניך is an idiom that can mean 'wise in your own eyes' (Prov 3:7). The English keeps 'in your eyes', as the Hebrew does.
הורינו אני וחבירי איך הדברים יעלו: the imperative is followed by a 'how' clause, so the English reads 'Instruct us ..., how the matters can agree'.
apparatus: Cf. Ezek 36:26 for 'ורוח חדש ניתן בקרבך' ('a new spirit ... within you'); the author does not quote it.
